questions.stem: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his brother because of a 5-day history of not sleeping and speaking so rapidly that the family cannot follow him. The brother says the patient has slept about 2 hours nightly since Saturday, has telephoned former coworkers at 3 AM to recruit them into a cryptocurrency venture that will ‘make this family untouchable,’ and purchased two vehicles and a boat on credit he does not have. He was found arguing with strangers outside a bank earlier today. He has never had a period of depressed mood, low energy, or loss of interest. He takes no medications, and he has no personal or family history of substance use. Urine toxicology screening is negative. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. On mental status examination, speech is rapid, pressured, and difficult to interrupt; he denies auditory or visual hallucinations and there are no delusions of reference. He is admitted to the inpatient psychiatric unit for safety. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: D. Major depressive disorder with mixed features
F. Substance/medication-induced bipolar and related disorder
questions.explanation: He has ≥3 DIGFAST symptoms (decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, impulsive spending, pressured speech, increased goal-directed activity, distractibility) — but only for 5 days. The buried clue is the last sentence: a manic episode is defined as ≥7 days OR any duration if hospitalization is required OR if psychosis is present, plus significant impairment. Admission for safety satisfies the criterion on its own → the 5-day count never has to reach 7. One manic episode = Bipolar I, and the explicit statement that he has never had a depressive episode is not a problem: depression is not required for Bipolar I. Board pearl — if a manic episode ever occurs, the diagnosis is Bipolar I permanently, no matter how much prior hypomanic or depressive history is documented.

wrongExplanations.0: Bipolar II requires ≥1 hypomanic episode plus ≥1 major depressive episode, and hypomania by definition involves no psychosis, no hospitalization, and no marked impairment. This patient was hospitalized and has never had a depressive episode, so both halves of the Bipolar II recipe fail.
wrongExplanations.1: Cyclothymic disorder requires ≥2 years of numerous hypomanic-level and depressive-level symptom periods that never meet full episode criteria, with symptom-free gaps never exceeding 2 months. This is a single 5-day episode meeting full manic criteria.
wrongExplanations.3: MDD with mixed features requires a major depressive episode as the primary episode, with manic/hypomanic symptoms layered onto it. He explicitly has never had depressed mood, low energy, or anhedonia.
wrongExplanations.4: Schizoaffective disorder requires ≥2 weeks of hallucinations or delusions in the absence of a mood episode. He has no psychotic symptoms at all — the mental status examination specifically records no hallucinations and no delusions.
wrongExplanations.5: A medication- or substance-induced episode requires an identified precipitant. He takes no medications, has no personal or family substance-use history, and urine toxicology screening is negative — three explicit negatives that close this option.

questions.eli5: He has been up for five days, talking fast, and buying boats he cannot pay for. Normally doctors want a week of that before calling it mania, but needing to go into the hospital counts instead of the week. One episode like that is all it takes to call it bipolar I.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the office at his brother's urging because of a 5-day period of sleeping about 4 hours nightly and speaking more rapidly than usual. The brother says that during this period the patient telephoned former coworkers about a business venture, closed two profitable contracts, and bought a used motorcycle he had been saving for and could comfortably afford. He went to work every day of that week and his supervisor described him as ‘unusually productive.’ Two years ago he had a 7-week period of depressed mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia, and a 15-lb weight loss during which he stopped attending his soccer league. He has never been psychiatrically hospitalized and has never had hallucinations or delusions. He takes no medications and urine toxicology screening is negative. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. On mental status examination, speech is mildly increased in rate but interruptible, and insight is intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: D. Major depressive disorder with mixed features
F. Substance/medication-induced bipolar and related disorder
questions.explanation: Same 5-day elevated-mood period, same symptom list — but every impairment marker is gone: he kept working, performed better than baseline, spent within his means, was never hospitalized, and had no psychosis. That is a hypomanic episode (≥4 days, no psychosis, no hospitalization, no marked impairment). Pair the hypomanic episode with the documented 7-week major depressive episode 2 years ago → Bipolar II disorder. Board pearl — Bipolar II is one of the very few DSM-5-TR diagnoses that does not require functional impairment, precisely because hypomania is non-impairing by definition; judge mania versus hypomania by extremity of consequence, not by the symptom list, which is identical for both.

wrongExplanations.1: Bipolar I requires at least one full manic episode — ≥7 days, or any duration with hospitalization or psychosis, plus significant impairment. This episode lasted 5 days with no hospitalization, no psychosis, and improved rather than impaired functioning, so it caps out at hypomania.
wrongExplanations.2: Cyclothymic disorder requires ≥2 years of subsyndromal highs and lows that never meet full episode criteria. His depressive episode 2 years ago was a full major depressive episode (7 weeks, anhedonia, weight loss, functional withdrawal), which disqualifies cyclothymia.
wrongExplanations.3: MDD with mixed features would require the current episode to be depressive with manic symptoms layered on. He is currently elevated, not depressed, and the depressive episode was a discrete event 2 years ago.
wrongExplanations.4: Schizoaffective disorder requires ≥2 weeks of psychosis in the absence of a mood episode. He has never had hallucinations or delusions.
wrongExplanations.5: He takes no medications and urine toxicology screening is negative, so there is no substance or medication to which the episode could be attributed.

questions.eli5: This is the same five fast days as the last patient, except nothing went wrong — he worked well, spent money he actually had, and never went to the hospital. That milder version is called hypomania, and hypomania plus a past bad depression equals bipolar II.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman comes to the office because ‘I've been down as long as I can remember.’ For the past 3 years she has had depressed mood on most days, poor concentration, low self-esteem, and a persistent sense of hopelessness, with no symptom-free stretch longer than about 3 weeks. She has continued to work full-time as a payroll clerk throughout. Over the past 4 weeks she has additionally stopped attending the church choir she previously enjoyed, lost 14 lb without dieting, and has awakened at 3 AM unable to return to sleep; she reports passive thoughts that she ‘wouldn't mind not waking up’ but has no plan or intent. She denies any period of decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, or elevated mood. She drinks one glass of wine weekly and urine toxicology screening is negative. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Serum TSH and complete blood count are within normal limits. On mental status examination, affect is constricted and psychomotor activity is mildly slowed; there are no delusions or hallucinations. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
C. Major depressive disorder, single episode, with melancholic features
E. Persistent depressive disorder with superimposed major depressive episode
questions.explanation: Two layers are stacked here. The chronic layer is persistent depressive disorder: depressed mood most days for ≥2 years (she has 3), with ≥2 of the milder criteria (poor concentration, low self-esteem, hopelessness) and never symptom-free for more than 2 months. The acute layer is a full major depressive episode in the past 4 weeks: ≥5 SIG E CAPS including anhedonia (quitting choir), appetite/weight change, early-morning awakening, psychomotor retardation, and suicidality. A full MDE riding on top of established PDD is called double depression. Board pearl — a normal TSH is doing real work here: hypothyroidism is the classic secondary cause that would reclassify this as a depressive disorder due to another medical condition rather than a primary one.

wrongExplanations.0: Adjustment disorder requires an identifiable stressor within the preceding 3 months and symptoms expected to resolve within 6 months of the stressor ending. No precipitant is described, and a 3-year course is far outside that window.
wrongExplanations.1: Cyclothymic disorder requires ≥2 years of alternating hypomanic-level and depressive-level symptoms. She explicitly denies any period of decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, or elevated mood, so the hypomanic half of the pattern is absent.
wrongExplanations.2: This label would capture only the past 4 weeks and would discard the 3 preceding years of continuous depressed mood — the chronic baseline is diagnostic information, not background noise, and it is exactly what converts this from a single episode into double depression.
wrongExplanations.3: PDD alone requires the milder, higher-functioning picture — roughly 3 criteria stretched over years. She now meets full major depressive episode criteria (≥5 symptoms including anhedonia and suicidal ideation), which PDD alone cannot account for.

questions.eli5: She has had a low grey mood for three years, like an overcast sky that never lifts. In the last month a real storm rolled in on top of it. Doctors call that stacked pattern double depression.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 5-month history of depressed mood. She sleeps 11 to 12 hours nightly and still naps in the afternoon, and her appetite has increased so much that she has gained 18 lb since March. She describes her arms and legs as feeling ‘filled with wet concrete’ for hours at a time, making it hard to get off the couch. She notes that her mood lifts noticeably and she becomes genuinely cheerful when her boyfriend visits or when she receives good news at work, though the improvement fades within a few hours. For the past several years, well before this episode began, she has abandoned friendships and turned down assignments after minor criticism from coworkers. Over the past 6 years she has had three similar episodes, two beginning in November and one beginning in mid-July. She denies suicidal ideation, hallucinations, and any period of elevated mood or decreased need for sleep. Serum TSH is 1.9 μU/mL and complete blood count is normal. On mental status examination, affect is reactive and psychomotor activity is normal. Which of the following specifiers best characterizes her current episode?
questions.explanation: Atypical features are defined by mood reactivity — the mood genuinely brightens in response to positive events — plus the ‘gains’: hypersomnia, hyperphagia with weight gain, leaden paralysis (limbs feeling weighted), and a longstanding pattern of interpersonal rejection sensitivity that is present outside episodes. All five are here. It is the trap of the name: atypical depression is actually the most common depressive subtype, not a rarity. Board pearl — melancholic and atypical are polar opposites in direction of travel: melancholic loses appetite, sleep, and pleasure (and the mood does not brighten for anything), while atypical gains weight and sleep and keeps its reactivity.

wrongExplanations.0: Anxious distress requires tension, restlessness, difficulty concentrating because of worry, fear of losing control, or fear that something awful will happen. None of these is described; her cognitive complaint is leaden heaviness, not worry.
wrongExplanations.2: Melancholic features require loss of mood reactivity — no brightening even for good news — along with early-morning awakening, weight loss, and marked psychomotor change. She sleeps too much, gained 18 lb, has normal psychomotor activity, and her affect is explicitly reactive: every element points the opposite way.
wrongExplanations.3: Mixed features require ≥3 manic/hypomanic symptoms present most days during the depressive episode. She specifically denies any period of elevated mood or decreased need for sleep.
wrongExplanations.4: The seasonal pattern specifier requires a regular temporal relationship between episode onset and time of year, with no off-cycle episodes. One of her three episodes began in mid-July — that single detail breaks the seasonal requirement and is the negative planted to eliminate this choice.

questions.eli5: When she is depressed she sleeps more, eats more, and her arms feel heavy like they are full of cement — but she can still cheer up for a few hours when something nice happens. That combination has a name: atypical depression, which is actually the most common kind.

questions.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes a depressive episode with a seasonal pattern from a depressive episode with atypical features?
choices: A. Hypersomnia accompanied by increased appetite and weight gain
B. Mood that brightens in response to positive events
C. A regular seasonal relationship between episode onset and remission
D. Onset of the first depressive episode before 25 years of age
E. Preferential response to bright-light therapy over an antidepressant
questions.explanation: Seasonal pattern is defined temporally, not symptomatically: episodes must begin and remit at characteristic times of year in a regular relationship, and there must be no episodes outside that window. Because seasonal episodes very often carry hypersomnia and hyperphagia themselves, symptom overlap with atypical features is heavy — the calendar is the only clean discriminator, which is why exam vignettes plant an off-cycle episode to rule seasonal pattern out.

wrongExplanations.0: Hypersomnia with increased appetite and weight gain is shared by both — it is a core atypical criterion and also the usual symptom picture of seasonal episodes, so it cannot separate them.
wrongExplanations.1: Mood reactivity is an atypical-features criterion, but it is not excluded in seasonal episodes and is not what defines the seasonal specifier.
wrongExplanations.3: Age of first onset is not part of either specifier's definition.
wrongExplanations.4: Treatment response is not a diagnostic criterion for any DSM-5-TR specifier; specifiers are assigned on presentation and course, not on what the episode responds to.

questions.eli5: Both kinds of depression can make you sleep and eat more, so symptoms will not tell them apart. The seasonal one is defined by the calendar: it shows up and goes away at the same time each year, every year.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man is brought to the office by his sister for evaluation. For the past 8 months he has believed that coworkers implanted a tracking chip in his shoulder, and he reports hearing two voices that comment on what he is doing. For the past 6 weeks he has additionally had depressed mood, has stopped playing guitar, has lost 20 lb, awakens at 4 AM, and reports passive thoughts of being better off dead. His sister states that for roughly 3 weeks in March, before any mood change began, ‘he was completely convinced about the chip and answering the voices out loud, but his mood was totally normal — he went out with friends, ate fine, slept fine, and was in good spirits.’ He has never had a period of decreased need for sleep or elevated mood. He takes no medications and urine toxicology screening is negative. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F) and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg; physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. On mental status examination, affect is blunted, speech shows increased response latency, and he intermittently glances toward the corner of the room. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: B. Bipolar I disorder, with psychotic features
D. Major depressive disorder, severe, with psychotic features
questions.explanation: The whole item turns on the sister's quote. Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with active psychosis PLUS a period of ≥2 weeks of hallucinations or delusions in the absence of a mood episode. The 3-week March window — psychosis fully present, mood explicitly normal with intact sleep, appetite, and socializing — supplies exactly that. He also now has a full major depressive episode overlapping the psychosis. Board pearl — ask ‘what is the baseline symptom?’ In a mood disorder with psychotic features, psychosis lives only inside the mood episode and disappears with it; in schizoaffective disorder, psychosis is the baseline and mood episodes are layered on top of it.

wrongExplanations.1: Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode. He has never had a period of decreased need for sleep or elevated mood, so no manic episode has ever occurred.
wrongExplanations.2: Delusional disorder requires a plausible fixed delusion as essentially the only psychotic feature, with preserved functioning and no prominent hallucinations. He has prominent auditory hallucinations, functional decline, and a superimposed mood episode.
wrongExplanations.3: This is the trap answer for a reader who registers only ‘depression plus psychosis.’ In MDD with psychotic features, the psychosis is confined to the depressive episode. Here the psychosis preceded any mood symptoms by about 4 months and persisted through a 3-week stretch of documented normal mood.
wrongExplanations.4: Schizophrenia requires that psychotic symptoms not be substantially accompanied by a concurrent major mood episode. He currently has a full 6-week major depressive episode overlapping his active psychosis, which pushes the diagnosis to the mood-linked psychotic disorder.

questions.eli5: He heard voices and believed in a tracking chip for months, and only later got very sad on top of it. There was a whole stretch where the voices were there but his mood was fine. When psychosis stands on its own like that and mood episodes come and go over it, doctors call it schizoaffective disorder.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium 900 mg PO twice daily for 11 years, with serum concentrations stable at 0.8 to 1.0 mEq/L on every check. She comes to the clinic because of a 6-day history of nausea, watery diarrhea, and a hand tremor that her husband says is ‘much bigger than the little shake she's always had,’ along with two episodes of stumbling into the door frame. In the past 2 weeks, following a dental extraction and a sinus infection, she began taking acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours, amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily, ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily, docusate sodium nightly, and caffeine tablets each morning to counter fatigue. She is afebrile; pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows a coarse bilateral hand tremor, mild gait ataxia, and no focal deficits or rigidity. Serum lithium concentration is 2.1 mEq/L, and serum creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL). Which of the following recently started medications is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Lithium is reabsorbed at the proximal convoluted tubule on the same sodium channels the kidney uses for salt, so anything that drives renal sodium retention drives lithium retention. NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis → decreased renal blood flow and increased proximal sodium reabsorption → decreased lithium clearance → rising levels. The rising creatinine (0.9 → 1.3 mg/dL) is the quiet confirmation that renal handling is the mechanism. Coarse tremor, ataxia, and GI upset at a level of 2.1 mEq/L are the toxicity picture. Board pearl — the level-raising list is thiazides, spironolactone, triamterene, ACE inhibitors, and NSAIDs; management is stop lithium, hydrate, and consider dialysis in severe cases.

wrongExplanations.0: Acetaminophen is not an NSAID, does not inhibit renal prostaglandins meaningfully at this dose, and has no established effect on lithium clearance — it is the deliberate near-miss for a reader who groups all analgesics together.
wrongExplanations.1: Amoxicillin has no recognized interaction with lithium. Metronidazole is the antibiotic on the lithium interaction list, and it increases nephrotoxicity rather than raising the level by this mechanism.
wrongExplanations.2: Caffeine moves lithium the wrong direction — like theophylline and aminophylline, it increases lithium excretion and lowers the level. If anything, stopping her caffeine would raise it.
wrongExplanations.3: Docusate is a stool softener with no meaningful lithium interaction, and her diarrhea is a symptom of the toxicity itself rather than evidence of a laxative effect.

questions.eli5: Lithium hitches a ride on the same kidney doors the body uses to hold onto salt. Ibuprofen makes the kidney hold onto more salt, so it holds onto more lithium too, and her level climbed until she got shaky and wobbly.

questions.stem: A patient who has taken lithium for 6 years has a bilateral hand tremor noted at every clinic visit. Which of the following features of the tremor most suggests that the current serum lithium concentration is in the toxic range?
choices: A. It is present only during voluntary movement toward a target
B. It is coarse rather than fine
C. It is symmetric in both hands
D. It becomes more noticeable after caffeine intake
E. It improves after a dose of propranolol
questions.explanation: A fine hand tremor is an expected effect of lithium at therapeutic concentrations (0.8 to 1.2 mEq/L) and does not by itself signal a problem. Coarsening of that tremor is one of the earliest clinical markers that the level has climbed into the toxic range (often above 1.8 mEq/L), and it typically travels with nausea, diarrhea, ataxia, slurred speech, and altered mental status. Board pearl — fine equals therapeutic, coarse equals toxic; the tremor is a built-in bedside level meter on a drug with a famously narrow therapeutic window.

wrongExplanations.0: An intention tremor that appears only on approach to a target points toward cerebellar pathology, not lithium concentration; lithium's tremor is a postural/action tremor present at rest with the arms extended.
wrongExplanations.2: Lithium tremor is symmetric at both therapeutic and toxic levels, so symmetry cannot separate the two. Asymmetry would instead raise suspicion for a different neurologic process.
wrongExplanations.3: Caffeine can accentuate any physiologic or drug-induced tremor and separately lowers lithium levels by increasing excretion, so worsening with caffeine argues against, not for, toxicity.
wrongExplanations.4: Beta-blocker responsiveness is a feature of the benign therapeutic tremor and of essential tremor; it tells you nothing about whether the serum concentration is toxic.

questions.eli5: A small, buzzy shake is normal on lithium. When the shake gets big and clumsy, the level in the blood has probably climbed too high.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man is seen for follow-up 3 weeks after a first manic episode that required hospitalization; he is now euthymic and wishes to begin maintenance pharmacotherapy. He has no other psychiatric history and no history of rash. He mentions only that ‘they told me my EKG was weird at a work physical years ago.’ He does not smoke and drinks no alcohol. Height is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) and weight is 76 kg (168 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m2. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, estimated GFR is 96 mL/min/1.73 m2, TSH is 2.1 μU/mL, aminotransferases are within normal limits, and absolute neutrophil count is 4,200/mm3. An ECG obtained today shows second-degree atrioventricular block, Mobitz type I. Which medication should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation: Lithium is the default first-line answer for bipolar maintenance, and this stem deliberately clears every objection you would normally raise against it: renal function is pristine, TSH is normal, and he cannot become pregnant. That is the decoy. The buried clue is the ECG. Cardiac conduction disease is one of the four named exceptions to lithium-as-default (the others being pregnancy, significant renal impairment, and difficult-to-manage thyroid disease), because lithium can further depress cardiac conduction. Board pearl — an ECG is part of the required lithium prescreening panel alongside CBC, creatinine/BUN, thyroid function, and serum hCG in women, and this is exactly why.

wrongExplanations.0: Aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist used for bipolar mania and maintenance with no conduction-system contraindication. Its relevant black-box warning concerns increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis, which does not apply to a 44-year-old.
wrongExplanations.1: Carbamazepine's disqualifying histories are bone marrow suppression and pregnancy. His absolute neutrophil count of 4,200/mm3 is normal, which is the negative planted to clear this option.
wrongExplanations.2: Lamotrigine's limiting risk is Stevens-Johnson syndrome from rapid titration, and he has no history of rash. It is generally the best-tolerated mood stabilizer and carries no conduction contraindication.
wrongExplanations.4: Quetiapine's main liabilities are sedation, orthostasis, and metabolic burden. His BMI of 24 kg/m2 makes metabolic risk a manageable consideration rather than a contraindication, and it does not affect AV conduction.
wrongExplanations.5: Valproate's contraindications are hepatic impairment and pregnancy. Normal aminotransferases are the explicit negative that rules this out, and valproate has no AV-conduction effect.

questions.eli5: Lithium is usually the go-to medicine after a manic episode, and all his kidney and thyroid tests look perfect. But his heart's electrical signal already has a delay in it, and lithium can slow that signal down even more — so this is the one drug to skip.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with bipolar I disorder maintained on olanzapine for 4 years was hospitalized for 3 weeks on a medical service for osteomyelitis, during which he could not smoke. He was discharged doing well. Three weeks after discharge he resumed smoking 1.5 packs of cigarettes daily, and 2 weeks later his wife brings him to the emergency department because he has stopped sleeping, believes his neighbors are broadcasting his thoughts, and has been pacing all night. His wife has watched him swallow each dose, and pharmacy records confirm on-time refills throughout. His serum olanzapine concentration is below the expected therapeutic range. Urine toxicology screening is negative and he drinks no alcohol. Which of the following best explains this patient's relapse?
choices: A. Nicotine competitively displaces olanzapine from plasma albumin
B. Cigarette smoke inhibits CYP1A2, slowing olanzapine metabolism
C. Cigarette smoke induces CYP1A2, accelerating olanzapine metabolism
D. Cigarette smoke induces CYP3A4, the primary enzyme metabolizing olanzapine
E. Nicotine is a dopamine partial agonist that opposes olanzapine's D2 blockade
questions.explanation: Olanzapine and clozapine are CYP1A2 substrates, and the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke — not the nicotine — are CYP1A2 inducers. Induction increases enzyme activity → substrate is metabolized faster → plasma level falls → loss of efficacy. Hospitalization removed the induction and his levels normalized; resuming 1.5 packs daily re-induced CYP1A2, olanzapine cleared faster, the level fell, and psychosis broke through. The dramatic decoy is the temptation to call this nonadherence, and the stem closes that door twice: witnessed dosing and on-time pharmacy refills. Board pearl — induction risks treatment failure, inhibition risks toxicity; roughly 95% of patients with psychotic disorders smoke, so this interaction is not an edge case.

wrongExplanations.0: Protein-binding displacement would transiently raise free drug, not lower total concentration, and nicotine does not meaningfully displace olanzapine from albumin. This distractor is built to sound pharmacologic without matching the measured low level.
wrongExplanations.1: This reverses the direction. Inhibition slows metabolism and raises the substrate level, which would produce sedation and side effects — the opposite of the low concentration and breakthrough psychosis actually documented.
wrongExplanations.3: The enzyme is wrong. Olanzapine's relevant pathway is CYP1A2; naming CYP3A4 is the vocabulary-plausible distractor for a reader who remembers that smoking induces something but not which isoenzyme.
wrongExplanations.4: Nicotine acts at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, not as a dopamine partial agonist, and a pharmacodynamic explanation cannot account for the measured drop in olanzapine concentration — the low level is the finding that forces a pharmacokinetic answer.

questions.eli5: Cigarette smoke speeds up the liver enzyme that chews through his medicine. In the hospital he could not smoke, so the medicine stuck around and worked. Once he was smoking again the liver burned through it too fast, the level dropped, and the illness came back even though he took every pill.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has been stable on imipramine 150 mg PO daily for 4 years for major depressive disorder. Two weeks ago her primary care physician started a medication to help her quit smoking. She is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because of 2 days of confusion, visual hallucinations of small animals, and picking at the air. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 148/90 mm Hg. Examination shows dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, absent bowel sounds, and 550 mL of retained urine on bladder scan. There is no muscle rigidity, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric throughout with no clonus. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 118 ms. Urine toxicology screening is negative and blood cultures are pending. Which of the following medications was most likely started 2 weeks ago?
questions.explanation: She has a full anticholinergic toxidrome — hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention, delirium with visual hallucinations — plus QRS widening, which is a tricyclic effect. She did not overdose; her imipramine dose never changed. Bupropion is a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor and imipramine is a CYP2D6 substrate → inhibition slows imipramine metabolism → levels climb toward supratherapeutic → anticholinergic delirium and cardiac conduction effects at an unchanged prescribed dose. Board pearl — the negatives are load-bearing: no rigidity excludes neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and normal reflexes with no clonus exclude serotonin syndrome, leaving the anticholinergic fever as the only one of the four fevers that fits.

wrongExplanations.1: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist used to blunt withdrawal symptoms; it causes sedation, bradycardia, and hypotension, not tachycardia with an anticholinergic toxidrome, and it has no CYP2D6 activity.
wrongExplanations.2: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist used for alcohol and opioid use disorder rather than smoking cessation, and it neither inhibits CYP2D6 nor produces anticholinergic findings.
wrongExplanations.3: Nicotine replacement delivers the same drug she was already getting from cigarettes and has no CYP2D6 effect. If anything, stopping the smoke itself would reduce CYP1A2 induction — which is not the pathway imipramine uses.
wrongExplanations.4: Varenicline is a partial agonist at the alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic receptor; its characteristic adverse effects are nausea and vivid dreams, and it does not inhibit CYP2D6 or cause anticholinergic delirium.

questions.eli5: Her old depression pill was fine for four years. The new quit-smoking pill jams the liver enzyme that clears the old one, so the old one piled up to about ten times its usual level and poisoned her — hot, dry, confused, and seeing things.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman who has taken sertraline 150 mg PO daily for 3 years for major depressive disorder is brought to the emergency department 18 hours after her surgeon started tramadol for postoperative pain following rotator cuff repair. She is agitated and reports abdominal cramping and four loose stools since the medication was started. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 122/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg. Examination shows moist, diaphoretic skin, hyperactive bowel sounds, and 6-mm pupils. Neurologic examination shows inducible ankle clonus bilaterally, 3+ patellar reflexes, and a fine tremor of both hands; muscle tone is normal with no lead-pipe rigidity. She has never taken an antipsychotic and has no history of malignant hyperthermia or exposure to inhaled anesthetics during this procedure, which was performed under a regional block. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: E. Hypertensive crisis from tyramine ingestion
questions.explanation: Serotonin syndrome is the fever with brisk neurology: onset within 24 hours of a serotonergic change (here tramadol added to sertraline — two different serotonergic mechanisms, which is where risk climbs fastest), plus the three A's of increased activity (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, diaphoresis, diarrhea), and altered mental status. Board pearl — clonus and hyperreflexia versus lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia is the single bedside discriminator between serotonin syndrome and NMS, and hours versus days is the second.

wrongExplanations.0: Anticholinergic toxicity produces dry, flushed skin and absent bowel sounds. Her skin is moist and diaphoretic and her bowel sounds are hyperactive with diarrhea — the exact opposite peripheral profile, which is why those two findings are stated explicitly.
wrongExplanations.1: Malignant hyperthermia follows exposure to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine and produces masseter and generalized rigidity with a rapid rise in end-tidal CO2. Her procedure was done under regional block with no inhaled agent, and her tone is normal.
wrongExplanations.2: NMS follows dopamine-blocking agents and develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity and diminished reflexes. She has never taken an antipsychotic, her onset was 18 hours, her tone is normal, and her reflexes are increased rather than decreased.
wrongExplanations.3: A sympathomimetic toxidrome from cocaine or amphetamine can mimic the vitals but does not produce inducible clonus with hyperreflexia, and there is no stimulant exposure — the temporal link is to a prescribed opioid analgesic.
wrongExplanations.4: Tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis is an MAOI-specific event requiring both an MAOI and an aged, fermented, or smoked food. She is on an SSRI, not an MAOI, and the trigger here is a drug rather than a meal.

questions.eli5: Her antidepressant and her new pain medicine both raise the same brain chemical, and together they pushed it too high within a day. Her reflexes went into overdrive — her ankles kept jerking — and she got hot, sweaty, and had diarrhea.

questions.stem: The patient in the preceding vignette has all serotonergic agents discontinued and receives lorazepam 2 mg IV twice along with external cooling and intravenous fluids. Four hours later her temperature is 38.9°C (102.0°F), she remains agitated, and sustained ankle clonus persists on examination. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: The management sequence for serotonin syndrome is stop the offending agents → benzodiazepines and supportive care including cooling and fluids → add cyproheptadine if there is no improvement. Cyproheptadine is a 5-HT2 receptor antagonist, so it acts directly against the mechanism driving the syndrome rather than merely sedating the patient. Board pearl — each of the four fevers has its own antidote, and matching them is a favorite exam move: serotonin syndrome takes cyproheptadine, NMS takes dantrolene or bromocriptine, MAOI hypertensive crisis takes phentolamine, and severe anticholinergic toxicity takes physostigmine.

wrongExplanations.0: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used to restore the central dopaminergic tone lost to an antipsychotic in NMS. There is no dopamine blockade in this patient, and adding a dopamine agonist does nothing for serotonin excess.
wrongExplanations.2: Dantrolene blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum to relax rigid muscle in NMS and malignant hyperthermia. Her muscle tone is normal, so there is no rigidity for it to treat, and it does not address serotonergic overactivity.
wrongExplanations.3: Phentolamine is the alpha-blocker used for the MAOI-tyramine hypertensive crisis. Her hypertension is one feature of generalized autonomic instability, not a catecholamine surge from tyramine, and alpha blockade leaves the clonus and hyperthermia untouched.
wrongExplanations.4: Physostigmine is the antidote for severe anticholinergic delirium. Giving a cholinesterase inhibitor here would worsen her already hyperactive bowel sounds and diaphoresis and could precipitate bradyarrhythmia.

questions.eli5: Stopping the medicines and giving calming drugs did not bring her fever or jerking reflexes down. Cyproheptadine blocks the exact receptor that the extra brain chemical is overstimulating, so it goes after the cause instead of just settling her down.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with treatment-resistant major depressive disorder was started on phenelzine 6 weeks ago after failing adequate trials of sertraline, venlafaxine, and nortriptyline. He is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after leaving a wedding reception because of a sudden, severe occipital headache that he describes as the worst of his life, along with palpitations, neck stiffness, and two episodes of vomiting. At the reception he ate aged cheddar, salami, and pickled herring. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 224/128 mm Hg. Examination shows 6-mm pupils bilaterally and diaphoresis. Muscle tone is normal, there is no rigidity, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout with no clonus. Noncontrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: MAOIs block the breakdown of monoamines, so dietary tyramine from aged, fermented, or smoked foods is absorbed intact and displaces norepinephrine from presynaptic vesicles → massive sympathetic surge → hypertensive crisis with diastolic pressure above 120 mm Hg, occipital headache, palpitations, neck stiffness, vomiting, diaphoresis, and mydriasis. Phentolamine, a nonselective alpha-adrenergic antagonist, directly opposes that surge. Board pearl — normal reflexes with no clonus and normal tone are the negatives that separate this from serotonin syndrome and NMS, which is exactly the discrimination the four-fevers table exists to test.

wrongExplanations.0: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist for NMS. He has taken no dopamine-blocking agent, has no rigidity, and is not hyperthermic — and a dopamine agonist would not counteract a noradrenergic surge.
wrongExplanations.1: Cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome, which requires hyperreflexia and clonus. His reflexes are 2+ with no clonus, and his trigger was a food rather than a serotonergic drug combination.
wrongExplanations.2: Dantrolene is used for the muscle rigidity and heat generation of NMS and malignant hyperthermia. His tone is normal and he is afebrile, so there is no rigidity-driven hyperthermia to treat.
wrongExplanations.4: Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, which presents with dry flushed skin and absent bowel sounds. He is diaphoretic, and giving a cholinesterase inhibitor during a hypertensive crisis adds cardiac risk without lowering the pressure.

questions.eli5: His antidepressant stops the body from breaking down a chemical found in aged cheese and cured meats. He ate a plateful of both, the chemical flooded in, and his blood pressure shot up with a pounding headache. Phentolamine blocks the receptors that surge is pushing on.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with major depressive disorder and chronic migraine is brought to the emergency department after her husband found her unresponsive beside an empty prescription bottle whose label had been removed. She has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure during transport. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. She is unresponsive to voice. Examination shows 7-mm pupils, dry flushed skin, and absent bowel sounds. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 152 ms and a prominent terminal R wave in lead aVR. Fingerstick glucose is 104 mg/dL. Urine toxicology screening is negative for opioids, benzodiazepines, cocaine, and amphetamines, and serum acetaminophen and salicylate concentrations are undetectable. Which of the following medications did she most likely ingest?
questions.explanation: This is the tricyclic overdose picture: the three C's — coma, convulsions, and cardiotoxicity — layered on a full anticholinergic toxidrome from M1 blockade. The buried clue is the ECG. Sodium-channel blockade widens the QRS beyond 100 ms and produces a terminal R wave in aVR, findings that belong to tricyclics and not to the other listed agents. Her chronic migraine is the quiet reason a tricyclic is in the house at all. Board pearl — tricyclics are lethal in overdose, classically described as carrying about a one-week supply of lethal drug, which is why they are avoided in patients at meaningful suicide risk.

wrongExplanations.1: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and carries a black-box warning for it, which makes the seizure the dramatic decoy in this stem. But bupropion does not produce QRS widening with a terminal R wave in aVR, and it does not cause an anticholinergic toxidrome with absent bowel sounds and urinary anticholinergic findings.
wrongExplanations.2: Mirtazapine overdose is characteristically benign, producing sedation, tachycardia, and disorientation. It does not cause seizures, sodium-channel-mediated QRS prolongation, or a dry anticholinergic toxidrome.
wrongExplanations.3: SSRI overdose alone is usually mild, producing nausea, tremor, and at most modest tachycardia. It causes neither this degree of coma with convulsions nor QRS widening.
wrongExplanations.4: Trazodone overdose causes profound sedation, orthostatic hypotension from alpha-1 blockade, and QT rather than QRS prolongation. Its signature adverse effect is priapism, and it does not produce the anticholinergic findings described.

questions.eli5: She swallowed a whole bottle of an old-style antidepressant she takes for migraines. Those drugs jam the sodium doors in the heart, so the heart's electrical beat gets stretched out wide on the tracing, and they also cause coma and seizures — that trio is the giveaway.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with major depressive disorder returns to the clinic after his third relapse in 2 years. He works rotating night shifts as a hospital security officer and reports missing 3 or 4 doses of medication most weeks because his sleep schedule shifts. Each of his previous relapses was attributed to gaps in therapy rather than lack of efficacy, and he tolerated his previous serotonergic agent without side effects. He has no obsessive-compulsive symptoms, no bulimia, and no seizure history. He takes no other medications. Pulse is 68/min and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg; ECG shows a QTc interval of 428 ms. Which of the following selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors is most appropriate for this patient?
questions.explanation: The constraint here is adherence, not efficacy — every agent listed would treat his depression. Fluoxetine has the longest half-life of the class (2 to 4 days) and an active metabolite, so a missed dose barely registers as a drop in plasma concentration; it is the SSRI specifically chosen for patients who cannot take medication reliably, and it can even be dosed weekly. Board pearl — the same half-life that makes fluoxetine forgiving also makes it the SSRI with the lowest discontinuation-syndrome risk, and it is a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor, so check the rest of the medication list before choosing it.

wrongExplanations.0: Citalopram carries a dose-dependent QTc prolongation warning and is the older, less clean member of its pair; more importantly, its intermediate half-life offers no protection against his missed doses.
wrongExplanations.1: Escitalopram is a reasonable antidepressant with no meaningful QTc effect, but its half-life is intermediate, so skipping 3 or 4 doses weekly still produces the trough-and-relapse pattern that has already failed him three times.
wrongExplanations.3: Fluvoxamine is FDA-approved for obsessive-compulsive disorder only and does not carry the general major depressive disorder indication the rest of the class does. The stem explicitly states he has no obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
wrongExplanations.4: Paroxetine has the shortest half-life in the class and the highest discontinuation-syndrome risk, making it the single worst choice for a patient who routinely misses doses — he would get flu-like symptoms and brain zaps every week.

questions.eli5: Every one of these medicines could treat his depression, so the real question is which one survives him forgetting it. Fluoxetine hangs around in the body for days, so a missed dose hardly changes anything.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the office because of an 8-month history of depressed mood, anhedonia, fatigue, poor concentration, guilt, and early-morning awakening; she denies suicidal ideation. She also reports that for the past 14 months she has eaten unusually large quantities of food in under 2 hours with a sense that she cannot stop, about five times weekly, each time followed by self-induced vomiting. She denies restricting her intake between episodes and denies laxative or diuretic use. She has never had a seizure. Height is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) and weight is 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 21.5 kg/m2. Pulse is 62/min and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg. Examination shows scarring over the dorsum of the right hand and mild parotid enlargement. Serum studies show K+ 3.2 mEq/L, Cl− 92 mEq/L, and HCO3− 32 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: She has bulimia nervosa (recurrent binge eating with recurrent compensatory purging, at least weekly for 3 months, at a normal BMI) plus comorbid major depressive disorder. Fluoxetine is the one agent on this list that carries an FDA indication for bulimia nervosa in addition to major depressive disorder, so a single drug treats both. Board pearl — the labs are not decoration: self-induced vomiting produces a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (low Cl−, low K+, high HCO3−), whereas laxative abuse produces an acidosis with low Na+ and high Cl−, and that acid-base split is a favorite way to confirm which purging method a stem is describing.

wrongExplanations.0: Bupropion carries a black-box contraindication in active or recent bulimia or anorexia nervosa because of seizure risk driven by purging-related electrolyte disturbance and dehydration. Her K+ of 3.2 mEq/L is precisely the derangement that warning exists for — if a stem describes bulimia and asks about a contraindicated drug, this is the answer.
wrongExplanations.2: Lithium requires a stable, consistent hydration state, and repeated self-induced vomiting creates a dehydration-prone state that raises the risk of lithium toxicity and nephrotoxicity. It also has no role in treating either bulimia or unipolar depression as monotherapy.
wrongExplanations.3: Mirtazapine's appetite stimulation and weight gain make it a reasonable choice in an underweight, insomniac patient, but it works against the goals of a patient with binge eating and normal BMI, and it has no bulimia indication.
wrongExplanations.4: Sertraline is the SSRI associated with binge eating disorder, which by definition involves no compensatory behavior. She purges after every binge, which makes this bulimia nervosa, and fluoxetine is the agent with that specific approval.

questions.eli5: She binges and then makes herself throw up, and she is also depressed. Fluoxetine is the one medicine here approved to treat both problems at once, and it avoids the drug that could give her a seizure because throwing up has already thrown off her body salts.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a painful erection that has lasted 5 hours. Three weeks ago he was prescribed a medication to be taken at bedtime for low mood accompanied by difficulty falling asleep. He has no history of sickle cell disease or other hemoglobinopathy, has never used intracavernosal injection therapy or a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, and urine toxicology screening is negative for cocaine and amphetamines. He has had no pelvic or perineal trauma. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Examination shows a rigid, tender penile shaft with soft glans. Which of the following medications was he most likely prescribed?
questions.explanation: All five options are sedating agents prescribed at bedtime for depressed mood with insomnia, so the option set gives nothing away. Trazodone blocks 5-HT2, H1, and alpha-1 receptors; alpha-1 blockade in the corpora cavernosa impairs detumescence → priapism, an erection lasting more than 4 hours and a urologic emergency. Board pearl — trazodone is used far more often as a hypnotic than as an antidepressant, because antidepressant efficacy requires doses high enough that sedation becomes limiting, and priapism is the adverse effect that must be disclosed at the time of prescribing.

wrongExplanations.0: Amitriptyline is a tertiary tricyclic with alpha-1, M1, and H1 blockade used for depression with chronic pain or migraine prophylaxis. Its sexual adverse effects are erectile difficulty and delayed ejaculation, not priapism.
wrongExplanations.1: Doxepin is a tertiary tricyclic used at low dose specifically for insomnia. It shares the tricyclic anticholinergic and antihistaminic profile but is not associated with priapism.
wrongExplanations.2: Mirtazapine is chosen for depression with insomnia and poor appetite through alpha-2, 5-HT2/5-HT3, and H1 antagonism. It causes sedation and weight gain and is notable for a low rate of sexual adverse effects overall.
wrongExplanations.3: Quetiapine has meaningful alpha-1 blockade and causes orthostatic hypotension and sedation, but priapism is the recognized signature of trazodone. The negatives in the stem — no sickle cell disease, no injection therapy, no stimulant use — exist to strip away every non-drug cause and force the drug answer.

questions.eli5: The medicine he takes at night for sleep and mood blocks a receptor that normally lets an erection go back down. When that switch is blocked, the erection can get stuck, which hurts and needs emergency treatment.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the office by her son because of an 8-month history of low mood, loss of interest in her book club, and poor appetite. She has lost 16 lb during that period and now lies awake from 3 AM onward. Height is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) and weight is 48 kg (106 lb); BMI is 18.6 kg/m2. She denies suicidal ideation, hallucinations, and any history of elevated mood. She lives alone, manages her own finances and medications, and scores 28/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Serum TSH is 2.4 μU/mL, vitamin B12 is 480 pg/mL, and complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel are within normal limits. She takes no medications. Pulse is 74/min and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg; ECG shows a QTc interval of 452 ms. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: Match the drug's adverse-effect profile to the symptoms you want to move. Mirtazapine is an alpha-2 antagonist that increases norepinephrine and serotonin release and also blocks 5-HT2, 5-HT3, and H1 receptors; the H1 blockade produces sedation and the 5-HT2/5-HT3 blockade drives appetite and weight gain. In a patient whose two most dangerous features are a 16-lb weight loss to a BMI of 18.6 kg/m2 and insomnia, those side effects are the therapeutic goal. Board pearl — the classic one-line pick is depression with insomnia and poor appetite equals mirtazapine, and the MoCA of 28/30 with preserved independent functioning is the negative that keeps this a mood disorder rather than a neurocognitive one.

wrongExplanations.0: Bupropion is activating and causes insomnia and weight loss. In a woman who has already lost 16 lb and cannot stay asleep, it pushes both of her worst problems further in the wrong direction.
wrongExplanations.1: Citalopram carries a dose-dependent QTc prolongation warning, and her QTc is already 452 ms — the buried clue in this stem. It also does nothing for her weight or sleep.
wrongExplanations.2: Duloxetine is a reasonable antidepressant and helps neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia, but she has no pain syndrome, and SNRIs tend to be appetite-neutral to appetite-suppressing rather than restorative.
wrongExplanations.4: Venlafaxine raises blood pressure at higher doses through norepinephrine reuptake inhibition, has a notably difficult discontinuation syndrome, and offers no benefit for her weight loss or insomnia.

questions.eli5: She is depressed, is not eating, and cannot stay asleep. Mirtazapine happens to make people sleepy and hungry, which are usually side effects to avoid but are exactly what she needs.

questions.stem: Which of the following selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors is FDA-approved for obsessive-compulsive disorder only and does not carry a general indication for major depressive disorder?
questions.explanation: Fluvoxamine is the exception within the SSRI class: its FDA labeling covers obsessive-compulsive disorder and does not include the general major depressive disorder indication every other SSRI carries. Board pearl — all six SSRIs are explicitly fair game, and each has one distinguishing fact worth holding onto: sertraline is the most prescribed and broadly indicated, fluoxetine has the longest half-life and adds bulimia and pediatric indications, escitalopram has no meaningful QTc effect, citalopram has dose-dependent QTc risk, paroxetine has the shortest half-life and the worst discontinuation syndrome, and fluvoxamine is OCD-only.

wrongExplanations.0: Citalopram is indicated for major depressive disorder; its distinguishing feature is dose-dependent QTc prolongation, not a restricted indication.
wrongExplanations.1: Escitalopram is indicated for major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder; it is the isomer of citalopram distinguished by the absence of a meaningful QTc effect.
wrongExplanations.2: Fluoxetine has the broadest label of the class — major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, bulimia nervosa, panic disorder, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and pediatric depression and OCD.
wrongExplanations.4: Paroxetine is indicated for major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, and PTSD; it is distinguished by having the shortest half-life and the highest discontinuation risk.
wrongExplanations.5: Sertraline is the most commonly prescribed SSRI, indicated for major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, PTSD, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and panic disorder.

questions.eli5: Almost every drug in this family is approved to treat depression. Fluvoxamine is the odd one out — it is officially only approved for obsessive-compulsive disorder.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the office by his mother because he has been telling relatives that a rival software company implanted receivers in his molars to capture his ideas before he can patent them. His mother states that this began in March and it is now August. He withdrew from his final semester of engineering school, quit his part-time job at a bicycle shop, and now leaves the apartment only to buy food. She says his speech has become hard to follow — "he starts on one thing and ends up somewhere else entirely." He reports hearing two voices that comment on what he is doing. He has never had a period of depressed mood, loss of interest, elevated mood, or decreased need for sleep. He takes no medications and has never used stimulants; urine toxicology screening is negative. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Serum TSH, complete blood count, and comprehensive metabolic panel are within normal limits, and noncontrast CT of the head shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, affect is flat, speech is tangential, and he has no insight into the belief about the receivers. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Do the arithmetic the stem hands you: March to August is 5 months, which lands squarely in the 1-to-6-month window for schizophreniform disorder. He meets psychosis criteria several times over (bizarre delusion, running-commentary auditory hallucinations, disorganized speech, flat affect as a negative symptom) and only one is required. The dramatic decoy is the severity — a failed semester, a lost job, near-total withdrawal, and a flat affect all feel like "real" schizophrenia, but functional decline is not the discriminator between these two; duration is, and he has not reached 6 months. Board pearl — brief psychotic, schizophreniform, and schizophrenia share identical symptom criteria and differ only on the clock: 1 day to 1 month, 1 to 6 months, and more than 6 months, so date arithmetic in the first sentence is never scenery.

wrongExplanations.0: Brief psychotic disorder requires at least 1 day but less than 1 month of symptoms. At 5 months he passed that ceiling four months ago.
wrongExplanations.2: Schizophrenia requires more than 6 months of continuous disturbance. He is at 5 months — if the mother had said February instead of March, this would be the answer, which is exactly why the month is stated twice.
wrongExplanations.3: Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with active psychosis. He explicitly has never had depressed mood, loss of interest, elevated mood, or decreased need for sleep, so there is no mood episode to concur with anything.
wrongExplanations.4: Delusional disorder requires a plausible, non-bizarre fixed delusion with otherwise preserved functioning and no prominent hallucinations. Implanted molar receivers is a bizarre delusion, he has running-commentary auditory hallucinations, and his functioning has collapsed.
wrongExplanations.5: Schizotypal personality disorder is a lifelong pattern of odd beliefs, magical thinking, and eccentric behavior without frank, fixed delusions or true hallucinations. His symptoms began at a datable point 5 months ago and include both.

questions.eli5: He truly believes there are radios in his teeth and he hears voices talking about him. Doctors put a stopwatch on this: under a month is one name, one to six months is another, and over six months is a third. He is at five months, so he gets the middle name.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man is on hospital day 3 after open reduction and internal fixation of an ankle fracture. Overnight he began pointing at the wall and describing insects crawling across it, and he pulled out his intravenous line twice. His wife says he drinks a pint of vodka every evening and had his last drink on the morning of admission. She adds that he had two seizures during a detoxification admission 6 years ago. He has no personal or family history of a psychotic disorder and has never taken an antipsychotic medication. He is afebrile, HR 122, BP 168/98, RR 22. He is diaphoretic and coarsely tremulous, is oriented to person only, and his attention fluctuates over the course of the interview. Fingerstick glucose is 118 mg/dL, urine toxicology screening is negative, there are no focal neurologic deficits or meningismus, and CT of the head shows no abnormalities. What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: This is delirium tremens on day 3 off alcohol — the "downers in withdrawal" half of the substance-psychosis rule, where the psychosis belongs to the withdrawal state and not to a primary psychotic disorder. A long-acting benzodiazepine is the answer because it is the only listed agent that is cross-reactive at GABA-A, and its active metabolites smooth the taper and lower the chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures. The buried clue is the pair of prior withdrawal seizures: that history makes seizure prevention the deciding constraint rather than an afterthought, and alcohol withdrawal is the single most lethal withdrawal syndrome precisely because of seizures and delirium tremens. Board pearl — the dramatic decoy here is the hallucination, which tempts an antipsychotic; treat the withdrawal and the hallucinations go with it.

wrongExplanations.1: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist that blunts the sympathetic surge of withdrawal and partially covers opioid and nicotine withdrawal, but it does not adequately prevent withdrawal seizures — which is exactly why it is never adequate monotherapy for CNS-depressant withdrawal, and exactly why his seizure history rules it out.
wrongExplanations.2: Haloperidol treats the surface complaint (the visual hallucinations) while leaving the GABA-A/NMDA rebound untouched, and it lowers the seizure threshold in a patient who has already had withdrawal seizures. He has no personal or family history of a psychotic disorder, so there is no primary psychosis for it to address.
wrongExplanations.3: Olanzapine has the same problem as haloperidol — it is a dopamine blocker aimed at a symptom rather than at the withdrawal physiology — and it adds sedation and metabolic burden without any seizure protection.
wrongExplanations.4: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures, which are generated by acute GABA-A/NMDA rebound rather than by a chronic epileptogenic focus; benzodiazepines, not phenytoin, are the agents shown to prevent them.

questions.eli5: His body got used to alcohol every night, and three days without it left his brain running way too fast — shaky, sweaty, and seeing bugs that are not there. A long-acting sedative from the same family calms the brain back down and, most importantly, stops him from having a seizure.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by campus police after he was found shouting at a parking-garage security camera, which he says has been transmitting his thoughts to a foreign government. His roommate reports 8 months of increasing isolation, a failed semester, and muttering to an unseen listener in their room. He takes no medications, urine toxicology screening is negative, and he has never used stimulants. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg; physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. He is admitted and started on haloperidol 5 mg PO twice daily, and over the next 4 days he stops responding to the voice and no longer mentions the camera. The improvement in this patient's symptoms is most directly attributable to dopamine blockade in which of the following pathways?
questions.explanation: The mesolimbic tract governs motivation and reward and is overactive in psychosis; excess dopamine here drives the positive symptoms — hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech and behavior. Blocking D2 receptors in this tract → reduced mesolimbic dopamine signaling → resolution of the voice and the camera belief. That is the therapeutic effect, and it is the only one of the four tracts where blockade is wanted. Board pearl — one receptor, four pathways, four different outcomes: block the mesolimbic tract and psychosis improves, and the other three blocks are your side-effect chapters.

wrongExplanations.0: The mesocortical tract handles cognition and motivation and is already underactive in psychosis. Blocking dopamine there worsens or fails to help negative and cognitive symptoms — it produces a problem rather than the benefit described.
wrongExplanations.1: The nigrostriatal tract runs the extrapyramidal motor system. Blockade there tips the striatal acetylcholine:dopamine balance toward relative cholinergic excess and produces EPS, not resolution of hallucinations.
wrongExplanations.3: The tuberoinfundibular tract is where dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release. Blockade there disinhibits prolactin and produces galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia, with no effect on psychotic symptoms.

questions.eli5: There are four dopamine highways in the brain. The medicine puts up a roadblock on all of them, but only one of those roadblocks is the one you actually wanted — the one that quiets the voices and the false beliefs.

questions.stem: Forty-eight hours after the first dose of haloperidol described in the preceding vignette, the same 21-year-old man's neck twists involuntarily to the left and his eyes deviate upward and remain fixed there. He is frightened and his speech is slurred. He is afebrile; pulse is 104/min and blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg. Muscle tone is increased in the neck and jaw only; there is no generalized rigidity, no diaphoresis, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout with no clonus. He denies any subjective urge to move and is able to sit still in the chair. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for these motor symptoms?
questions.explanation: Sudden, sustained muscle contraction — here torticollis plus oculogyric crisis — within hours to days of a high-potency typical is an acute dystonic reaction, and young men on first exposure are the classic highest-risk group. D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal tract → relative cholinergic excess in the striatum → sustained contraction, so the fix is an anticholinergic given by a route that works in minutes. Benztropine 2 mg IM is that answer, and the relief is often dramatic. Board pearl — the whole option set here is correct drugs at wrong routes or for wrong EPS subtypes: in acute dystonia, the route is as much of the answer as the molecule, because dysarthria and jaw involvement can progress to laryngeal spasm.

wrongExplanations.0: Amantadine is a dopamine agonist used for pseudoparkinsonism, not for acute dystonia, and an oral agent takes far too long for a reaction that is already involving his jaw and speech.
wrongExplanations.1: Diphenhydramine is the right pharmacologic idea — it is the antihistamine alternative to benztropine for dystonia — but by mouth it is too slow, and 25 mg PO will not abort an oculogyric crisis in progress.
wrongExplanations.2: Stopping the antipsychotic does nothing for the contraction already occurring and leaves an acutely distressed patient with jaw and speech involvement untreated. Stopping the drug is the first step for tardive dyskinesia and for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not for acute dystonia — and he is afebrile with no generalized rigidity, so this is neither.
wrongExplanations.4: Propranolol is first-line for akathisia. He explicitly denies any urge to move and can sit still, which is the negative that removes akathisia from consideration.
wrongExplanations.5: Trihexyphenidyl is an appropriate anticholinergic for drug-induced parkinsonism and can be used chronically, but the oral route is too slow for an acute dystonic reaction.

questions.eli5: His neck locked to one side and his eyes rolled up and stuck there two days after starting the new medicine. A shot of an anticholinergic in the muscle unlocks it within minutes — a pill would take too long while his jaw and voice are already involved.

questions.stem: The dystonic reaction described above resolves within 20 minutes. Three weeks later the same patient, now maintained on haloperidol 5 mg PO twice daily with continued improvement in his delusions, tells the nurse that he feels "like my legs have to go somewhere." He is observed rocking from foot to foot at the medication window and cannot remain seated through a 20-minute group session; he stands and paces four times. He denies depressed mood, denies worry about any specific thing, and denies any return of the belief about the camera. He is afebrile; pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. There is no tremor at rest, no cogwheel rigidity, and no orofacial or lingual movement. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Add benztropine 1 mg PO twice daily
B. Add propranolol 20 mg PO three times daily
C. Increase haloperidol to 10 mg PO twice daily
questions.explanation: Subjective inner restlessness plus visible inability to sit still, arriving days to weeks into a high-potency typical, is akathisia, and propranolol is classically first-line; benzodiazepines are the usual second option. The trap is that akathisia is the one EPS syndrome that does not respond well to the anticholinergic reflex that works for dystonia and pseudoparkinsonism — reaching for benztropine here is the single most common wrong move. His stated negatives do real work: no depressed mood and no focused worry separate akathisia from agitation and anxiety, and no tremor, rigidity, or orofacial movement separate it from pseudoparkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia. Board pearl — akathisia is dose-related, so escalating the antipsychotic to "cover the restlessness" makes the very side effect you are treating worse.

wrongExplanations.0: Benztropine is the classic choice for acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, but it is a distinctly less reliable treatment for akathisia specifically than a beta-blocker — and he has neither tremor nor rigidity for it to address.
wrongExplanations.2: Akathisia is a dose-related consequence of striatal D2 occupancy climbing past the roughly 78-80% EPS threshold. Doubling the dose pushes occupancy higher and predictably worsens the restlessness, and his delusions are already improving, so there is no efficacy reason to escalate.
wrongExplanations.3: This is the sophisticated-sounding switch that the data do not support: the aripiprazole-family partial agonists carry some of the highest reported akathisia rates of any antipsychotics, so switching to one to treat akathisia risks trading sideways at best.
wrongExplanations.4: Chlorpromazine is a low-potency typical with less EPS, but switching agents abandons a medication that is working on his psychosis to treat a side effect that has a simple, effective, first-line drug — and it buys a heavy anticholinergic, sedating, alpha-blocking burden instead.

questions.eli5: He is not anxious and he is not sad — his body just will not let him sit down. That specific side effect is treated with a beta-blocker, not with the anticholinergic that fixed his neck three weeks ago, and definitely not by raising the dose that caused it.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with schizophrenia is being switched to a different antipsychotic because of persistent auditory hallucinations on her current agent. She has had three episodes of syncope in the past year, two of them while walking. She takes furosemide for lower-extremity edema. She is afebrile, HR 68, BP 118/72, RR 14. Serum K+ is 3.2 mEq/L and Mg2+ is 1.6 mg/dL. ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc interval of 486 ms. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2, fasting glucose is 88 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c is 5.2%. She has never had agranulocytosis or any drug-induced movement disorder, and she is not pregnant. What medication should be avoided by the prescriber in this case?
questions.explanation: Every option on this list would treat her psychosis, so the psychiatric picture is scenery and the decision is made entirely by the cardiac data. Ziprasidone carries the strongest QT-prolongation signal among the atypical antipsychotics, and she arrives with a QTc of 486 ms plus a loop diuretic driving hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia — three additive risks for torsades in a woman already having syncopal episodes. Board pearl — the decoy is that ziprasidone is one of the metabolically cleanest atypicals, so a reader ranking these agents by weight gain picks it as the safe choice; her normal BMI, glucose, and A1c are the planted negatives that make metabolic risk irrelevant here and force the QT axis instead.

wrongExplanations.0: Aripiprazole sits at the lowest-risk end of the QT-prolongation table along with lurasidone, and it is also lowest for metabolic burden and prolactin elevation. There is nothing in this stem that argues against it.
wrongExplanations.1: Clozapine's disqualifying histories are agranulocytosis and its monitoring burden, and the stem explicitly states she has never had agranulocytosis. Its risks are hematologic, seizure-related, and cardiac in the myocarditis sense, not QT interval prolongation.
wrongExplanations.2: Lurasidone shares the lowest-QT slot with aripiprazole and carries low metabolic risk, making it one of the more reasonable choices for exactly this patient rather than the one to avoid.
wrongExplanations.3: Olanzapine's liability is metabolic — the highest weight gain and type 2 diabetes risk of the class alongside clozapine. Her BMI of 23 kg/m2, fasting glucose of 88 mg/dL, and A1c of 5.2% are the explicit negatives that neutralize that concern.
wrongExplanations.4: Risperidone's signature problems are frequent hyperprolactinemia and, as a "-done," more EPS than the "-pines." The stem states she has never had a drug-induced movement disorder and she is not pregnant, and neither issue involves the QT interval.

questions.eli5: All six of these medicines would help her hear fewer voices, so the choice comes down to her heart tracing, which already shows a long reset time. One of the six stretches that reset even longer, and her water pill has dropped her body salts, which makes it riskier still.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-month history of absent menstrual periods and a milky discharge from both nipples that she first noticed on her shirt. She began an antipsychotic 5 months ago for schizophrenia, and her auditory hallucinations have resolved completely. Her BMI is 22 kg/m2, unchanged from before she started the medication. She takes no other prescription medications, herbal products, or over-the-counter agents, and she has had no head trauma. Urine pregnancy test is negative, serum TSH is 1.8 μU/mL, and visual fields are full to confrontation. Serum prolactin is 96 ng/mL. She has had no tremor, rigidity, or restlessness. Which of the following antipsychotics is she most likely taking?
questions.explanation: Work backward from the effect. Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release through the tuberoinfundibular tract, so D2 blockade there → disinhibited prolactin → galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. Among the atypicals, risperidone and its active metabolite paliperidone sit at the top of the prolactin-elevation table, and risperidone is the agent classically described as causing frequent hyperprolactinemia. The stated negatives are load-bearing and each closes a competing explanation: a negative pregnancy test, a normal TSH, and full visual fields eliminate pregnancy, hypothyroidism, and a chiasm-compressing prolactinoma. Board pearl — the unchanged BMI is the quiet detail that steers you away from the "-pines": the famous antipsychotic side effect is weight gain, and its absence here is what makes prolactin the axis in play.

wrongExplanations.0: Aripiprazole sits at the lowest-risk end of the prolactin table — as a D2 partial agonist it stabilizes rather than fully blocks dopamine tone, so it is the agent least likely to produce hyperprolactinemia, and it is often used to reverse it.
wrongExplanations.1: Clozapine has essentially no prolactin elevation, which is one of its notable "unique lack of side effects" alongside its absence of EPS and tardive dyskinesia. Its problems are agranulocytosis, seizures, sialorrhea, myocarditis, and heavy metabolic burden.
wrongExplanations.2: Olanzapine is a "-pine" whose signature adverse effects are weight gain, sedation, and metabolic syndrome. Her BMI is explicitly unchanged at 22 kg/m2, and olanzapine is not a leading cause of hyperprolactinemia.
wrongExplanations.3: Quetiapine has essentially no prolactin elevation. Its recognizable liabilities are sedation from H1 antagonism, orthostatic hypotension, and metabolic burden.

questions.eli5: Dopamine normally acts like a lid on the hormone that makes breast milk. Her medicine blocks dopamine, the lid comes off, milk shows up and her periods stop — and one medicine in this list is far more likely than the others to do that.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken olanzapine 20 mg PO daily for 2 years, with complete resolution of his auditory hallucinations and persecutory beliefs and no missed doses documented on pharmacy refill records. He has gained 38 lb (17 kg) during that period, and his BMI has risen from 26 to 33 kg/m2. Blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Fasting serum glucose is 152 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c is 7.9%, and serum triglycerides are 310 mg/dL; both glucose and A1c were normal before he started the medication. ECG shows a QTc interval of 402 ms. He has had no extrapyramidal symptoms, no galactorrhea, and no sedation that interferes with his work. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Continue olanzapine and add metformin
questions.explanation: He has developed frank type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia on the antipsychotic that, with clozapine, anchors the highest-risk end of the metabolic table. When diabetes or substantial weight gain emerges on an antipsychotic, consensus guidance is to move the patient to an agent at the low-risk end rather than to layer a second chronic medication on top of the cause — and aripiprazole shows up on the "lowest risk" side of nearly every side-effect row, with the cleanest metabolic profile of the group. Board pearl — diabetes risk in psychiatric patients already runs 2 to 4 times the general-population baseline before any drug is added, and ziprasidone is the other guideline-named low-metabolic switch, though its QT signal has to be checked first.
